opening.title: Before the ninth night
panels: Bellwether. A fishing town on the Pacific coast.
Six thousand people, one radio station, and a lot of fog.
I’m Steve Mercer. For twelve years I ran the night shift at KBWR, the town radio station.
Nobody hears the night engineer. The night engineer hears everything.
My dad, Frank, taught me how to listen. Every sound has a source, he used to say. Go and find it.
Ham radio, every night. Strangers from all over the world, all of them his friends.
My mom, Helen, was an interpreter. Government work, rooms with no windows. She never talked about it.
She could hear what people meant, even when they said something else.
Eighteen months ago, they rowed out into the bay after dark. They said the water was making a sound.
They asked me to come along.
I said no. I had a shift.

aftermath.title: Eighteen months
panels: In the morning, their boat drifted back to shore. Empty.
Dad’s radio was still on.
Nobody found them. That was eighteen months ago.
Mom called me from the boat that night. I kept her voicemail on a cassette. Most nights I play it at three in the morning. I don’t know what I’m listening for.
A year ago a company called Halcyon Media bought KBWR.
Three weeks ago they replaced me with a machine called DJ AutoRick. It reads yesterday’s weather.
And then there’s Nora. Nora Reyes runs the animals at the aquarium and argues with everybody, me included.
After the boat I went quiet. She pushed, then shouted, then stopped. Lately she’s been endlessly patient with me. I figured I’d worn her out.
So now I’m home in the mornings, with Dad’s old tape recorder and nothing left to fix.
This is the story of how I started counting nights.

p_bay.when: Eighteen months ago, a little after eleven at night
p_bay.objective: Help Frank find the hum hiding under his radio static.
p_bay.coach: Click the glowing radio to begin. Press I for a list of things to look at.
notes: Mix a faint low hum (the ship) under the voicemail recording.voicemail. Chapter 1 depends on hearing it there.

intro.text: Nine nights since the last one, Helen. Same interval. Louder out here. Whatever it is, it keeps better time than I do.

tune.goal: Find the hum between the two stations.
tune.background: Frank has tracked a hum under his radio static for months. It comes every ninth night, and out on the water it is louder. Two stations crowd the band: a time signal on one side, a chime on the other.
tune.prompt: Drag the dial until both stations fade, switch on Narrow bandwidth, then record what is left.
hints: Drag the dial toward the middle, away from both stations.
The hum sits in a quiet gap between the two stations. Narrow bandwidth shuts out their edges.
Stop where both stations are at their faintest, in the low 800s. Switch on Narrow bandwidth before you record.
tune.finding: frank|K7BLW log, eleven-oh-four. Eight-fifteen, narrow band. Not one tone. Several, holding the same note.

message.title: Helen’s phone
message.goal: Get the hum onto Steve’s voicemail.
message.background: Steve stayed ashore for his shift at KBWR. Helen wants him to hear this for himself, but her phone’s little microphone won’t pick up the radio from across the boat.
message.prompt: Where should Helen hold the phone while she leaves Steve a message?
options: Up in the wind, away from the radio
Inside her coat, out of the spray

wrong.1: The wind would swallow everything but her voice.
wrong.2: Warm and dry, but all he’d hear is wool.

hints: The phone has to hear the radio, not just Helen.
Which spot is closest to the sound she wants Steve to hear?
The phone should sit as close as it can to the sound Helen wants Steve to hear, not to Helen.

lines.text: He should hear this for himself. There. Now he’ll tell us we recorded it wrong.

message.finding: frank|Eleven-twenty. Helen called the boy. Held the phone to my speaker, so he gets the hum along with her.

recap: frank|Eleven-forty. The note is climbing. Helen says it has a shape, like speech. We’re going to follow it out.
p_bay.next: Black. The storybook “Eighteen months” plays, then Chapter 1.

lines: frank|Think the boy will come out with us next time?
helen|He’ll say he has a shift. Then he’ll call tomorrow and ask what we heard.
frank|He always asks.
helen|He’s your son, Frank. He can’t leave a sound alone.
helen|My hands are freezing.
frank|Gloves are in the tackle box. Under the logbook.
helen|Of course they are. Everything in this boat is under the logbook.
helen|Listen. It goes up at the end, like a question.
frank|Then write it down. Time, place, what it does.
helen|Eleven-oh-five. Rowboat. It sounds like it’s waiting for someone.

c1_flat.when: Saturday the 20th, three in the morning, then Sunday morning

chapter.title: Good Morning, Sleepyhead
chapter.when: Saturday the 20th, three in the morning
chapter.goal: Steve wants to save his mother’s last voicemail before the tape wears out.

c1_flat.objective: Test Dad’s old recorder before you move Mom’s voicemail to a fresh tape.
c1_flat.coach: Click the red cassette to begin. Click Nora if you want to chat. Press J to open Steve’s notebook.
notes: New sound: effect.kbwr_ident, Steve’s 12-second KBWR station ident. The tape-alignment strips must show the ident followed by the greeting, so the player lines the tapes up on the ident first.
Red cassette = Saturday, blue cassette = Sunday, silver recorder = the tape test, headphones and reels = the comparison. These match the painting.
intro: steve|Your tape’s wearing thin, Mom. I’ll move you to a fresh one. Just as soon as Dad’s recorder runs true.

intro.new: steve|Dad’s recorder runs slow. Old belts. Everyone on it sounds a little sleepy.
steve|There’s an easy test. KBWR still plays my old station ident at a quarter past seven every morning. I made that ident. It runs exactly twelve seconds.
steve|Record it two mornings running. If it lasts twelve seconds both times, the machine runs true.

saturday.title: The red cassette
saturday.goal: Catch something on tape that never changes.
saturday.background: To time Dad’s recorder, Steve needs a sound that is exactly the same every time it plays. The kitchen radio is tuned to KBWR, where AutoRick plays Steve’s twelve-second station ident at 7:15 every morning.
saturday.prompt: Saturday morning. What should the red cassette catch at a quarter past seven?
options: The KBWR station ident on the kitchen radio
Steve reading the same sentence aloud

wrong.1: My voice changes every time I open my mouth. A reference can’t change.
wrong.2: Nora grinds the beans differently every day. That’s sort of the point of Nora.

hints: Steve needs a sound that is identical every time it plays.
A person never does anything exactly the same way twice. A recording does.
Only one of the three sounds comes off a station cart, exactly the same every morning.
lines: c1_flat.in.04
steve|Morning, Nor.
c1_flat.saturday.01
iris|Coffee’s on the stove. I made it strong, the way you like it.
steve|You hate it strong.
iris|Strong is fine. Whatever you like.
saturday.finding: steve|Red cassette, Saturday, 7:15. My ident, AutoRick, Nora saying good morning on her way out, and me.

sunday.title: The blue cassette
sunday.goal: Record the second reference exactly like the first.
sunday.background: A fair test changes one thing only: the day. If anything else moves, the recorder, the volume or the time, a difference on the tape could come from that instead.
sunday.prompt: Sunday, 7:14. How should Steve set up the blue cassette?
options: Same spot on the table, same level, record at 7:15
Next to the radio, so the ident comes out louder
Wait and record the noon news instead

wrong.1: Then a difference could just be the distance. Change one thing, and only one.
wrong.2: The news is new every day. Only the ident repeats.

hints: Repeat Saturday’s test exactly.
Anything that changes besides the day spoils the comparison.
Two of the setups move something besides the day: the distance, or the sound itself.

lines.new: autorick|The voice of the coast, now with zero humans!

lines.text: Morning, Nor. Blue tape, Sunday. Date on everything, Dad.

lines: iris|I’m off to feed Admiral and the otters. Back by noon.
steve|On a Sunday? You used to fight for every Sunday off.
iris|The animals don’t know it’s Sunday, sleepyhead.
sunday.finding: steve|Blue cassette, Sunday, 7:15. The ident, the radio, Nora and me, all over again. Now I can time the machine.

compare.title: Two mornings, side by side
compare.goal: Line the two cassettes up on the ident and time Dad’s recorder.
compare.background: Steve puts the red cassette in one ear and the blue in the other. If the recorder runs true, the two idents will line up. The tapes also caught the rest of the kitchen: AutoRick on the radio, Nora on her way out, and Steve himself.
compare.prompt: Slide Sunday until the two idents line up. Then play both tapes and compare every voice on them.
compare.instruction: First line up the ident. Then listen to each voice on both tapes and say how the two days compare.

rows.label: The ident
options: Same words, said a new way

rows.label: AutoRick
options: Same words, said a new way

rows.label: Steve: Morning, Nor.
options: Same words, said a new way

rows.label: Nora: Good morning, sleepyhead.
options: Same words, said a new way

hints: Line up the end of the ident first. Then play both tapes together.
AutoRick reads a new script every day. A person says the same words a little differently each time.
Only a recording repeats every breath and click. Compare each voice with the ident.

lines.text: Twelve seconds, both days. Dad’s recorder runs true.

lines: steve|And Nora... lines up too. The breath. The little click before “morning.”
steve|Nobody says a sentence the same way twice. I spent twelve years listening for exactly that.
compare.finding: steve|The ident matches, so the recorder is fine. AutoRick and I change from day to day, like anyone would. Nora’s good morning matches perfectly. People don’t do that. Recordings do.

control.title: Dad’s recorder
control.goal: Rule out the most boring explanation first.
control.background: Steve’s notebook rule: list every explanation, then cross them out, starting with the dull ones. Dad reused his cassettes for years. An old tape can carry a ghost of an earlier recording.
lead: c1_flat.out.02
steve|Let’s not panic yet. Let’s make a list.
control.prompt: Steve says “one, two” twice onto the blue cassette, and a chair squeaks only during the second pass. On playback the squeak is there once, and nothing of Saturday plays underneath. Which explanation can he cross out?
options: The blue tape carried Saturday’s sound over
I was tired and heard a match that was never there
Since the boat, I’ve been reading too much into ordinary things

wrong.1: The squeak tests the tape, not my ears. Tiredness stays on the list for now.
wrong.2: The squeak says nothing about grief. It’s about the tape. That one stays on the list too.

hints: Which explanation is about the machine?
A tape carrying old sound would play Saturday underneath, or repeat the first pass. It did neither.
A ghost of Saturday would sound like Saturday. Did anything from Saturday play under the test?
lines: c1_flat.control.01

lines.text: The squeak made the second pass only. Nothing of Saturday underneath. So the tape is clean. Cross that one out.

control.finding: steve|Crossed out: the tape. It holds only what happened in the room. That leaves my ears, my grief, or Nora.

recap: steve|Dad’s recorder runs true, and the tape is clean. And the woman I love said good morning twice, the way a cassette would.
steve|I tried to remember our last real conversation. I couldn’t. Before the boat, she never said anything the same way twice.
outro: steve|Nor? Walk the pier with me this afternoon? Like we used to. We could say hi to Admiral.
iris|And Mamá kept your plate warm again. Dinner at six, if you want.

lines: steve|Want some toast before you go?
iris|I ate already. There’s fruit in the blue bowl.
steve|Since when do you eat breakfast?
iris|For a while now. It’s good for you.
steve|How are the otter pups?
iris|Growing. One of them bit a volunteer again. Only a little.
steve|You used to say that was her best quality.
iris|She’s a good otter. They’re all good otters.
iris|I heard the new radio host this morning. He sounds cheerful.
steve|He read yesterday’s weather again. Twelve years at that desk, and they replaced me with him.
iris|Then you have more time at home. That’s nice, isn’t it?
steve|Sure, Nor. Nice.
steve|Nor? How did you sleep?
iris|Fine. I always sleep fine.
steve|You used to kick the blankets off every night. Every single night.
iris|Did I? I don’t remember that.

c1_pier.objective: Spend the afternoon on the pier with Nora.
c1_pier.coach: Click people to chat. Some leads open a case board: pick a card, then pick the question it answers, and press Check.
notes: New sounds: effect.harbor_winch; effect.nora_whistle_flat (her two notes, the second falling); effect.steve_whistle (breathy and clumsy, but the second note rises like the real one).
Art (optional): an insert of Admiral hauling out beside Steve, matching inserts/c1_pier.webp.
context: steve|Sunday on the harbor. The crab boats were in, the winch was hauling pots onto the dock, and the fish shed had a line out the door.
steve|Every Sunday, Nora visits Admiral, the sea lion she raised from a rescued pup. I used to come along.
steve|I hadn’t, in a long time.
steve|Sheriff June Calder was in that fish-shed line, the way she is every Sunday. Mrs. Penhallow sat at her bait stall, where nobody ever buys anything.

intro.text: Admiral! That was my lunch. You’re six hundred pounds of sea lion, and you don’t even like rye.

whistle.title: Admiral’s whistle
whistle.goal: Give Admiral a fair chance to hear Nora’s whistle.
whistle.background: Admiral has come to Nora’s two-note whistle since the day she bottle-fed him. He steals food from everybody else. Right now he is underwater, and the harbor winch is roaring.
lead: steve|Your whistle, Nor. He always comes for that.
steve|He didn’t even come up. The winch is going. He probably didn’t hear you.
whistle.prompt: Steve is worried Admiral might be sick. How can he give Admiral a fair chance to answer her?
options: Wait until the winch stops and Admiral surfaces, then ask Nora to whistle again
Toss Admiral the rest of the sandwich

wrong.1: That only tests whether he likes rye. He doesn’t, and he’d eat it anyway.
wrong.2: Then he’d be answering me. I want to know if he hears her.

hints: What else could keep Admiral from hearing her?
Take away the winch and the water before you trust the result.
A fair test removes every excuse: the noise, and the water between them. Then Nora gets another try.

lines.new: steve|Nothing. He’s looking right at you.
steve|...He came for me. I can’t even whistle.

lines: iris|He wants the rest of your sandwich.
whistle.finding: steve|Admiral hears fine. He came to my clumsy whistle and turned away from Nora’s. Her second note went down. It always used to go up.

door.title: Deputy Lyle
door.goal: Put a date on Lyle’s change of heart.
door.background: Deputy Lyle Boone took the missing-persons report on Steve’s parents and never called him back. Since his divorce he has missed most of his sons’ games. Dad’s rule: put a date on everything.
lead: lyle_copy|Steve. I owe you an apology. When your folks went missing, I never called you back. That wasn’t right.
steve|...Thank you, Lyle.
c1_pier.door.01
door.prompt: Lyle Boone has never apologized for anything. What does Steve ask him?
options: “Since when do you make their games?”
“Who are you, and what have you done with Lyle?”

wrong.1: That’s an accusation. He’d close up, and I’d learn nothing.
wrong.2: He’d laugh, I’d laugh, and I’d learn nothing. Put a date on it.

hints: A change only matters once you know when it happened.
Lyle will happily tell Steve about his new habit. Ask how long he’s had it.
Lyle loves talking about his boys. A question about when the new habit started gets a date, not a fight.
lines: lyle_copy|Every one since June. Haven’t missed one. Ask the boys.
c1_pier.door.02
door.finding: steve|Lyle Boone has gone to every game since June. Before that he missed them all. And he apologized to me.

bait.title: Agnes’s bait stall
bait.goal: Work out where the low note is coming from.
bait.background: Mrs. Agnes Penhallow taught Steve in third grade. She is ninety-one and sells bait that nobody buys. Today a low note is drifting in off the water, and she is humming along. Steve knows that note. It is under Mom’s voicemail.
lead: c1_pier.in.02

lead.new: steve|That note. It’s under Mom’s voicemail. I always thought it was the phone line.

lead: agnes|It’s loud today, Steven. It always is, on certain nights.
steve|June! Did you hear that hum just now?
calder|From the fish-shed line. It started before Agnes did.
calder|It was loudest down by the water, under the floating dock.
steve|Could you hear Agnes humming from there?
calder|Nobody can hear Agnes hum. She’s quieter than the fog.

lead.new: steve|And the winch stopped halfway through. The note just kept going.

bait.prompt: Every sound has a source. Is the low note Agnes, or something else?

board.instruction: Agnes keeps a tide book in her bait tin. Help her answer four questions about the low note.
evidence: June was in the fish-shed line. She heard the low note before Agnes started humming.
June could not hear Agnes from the fish shed.
June heard the note best by the water, under the floating dock.
The winch stopped halfway through the note. The note kept going.

stages.prompt: Put one card on each question.
slots: Where does the low note come from?
What stopped before the note did?
Who heard the note without Agnes?

board.wrong_text: Something here doesn’t match Agnes’s tide book yet.

hints: Start with June. What did she hear, and where was she?
A sound that stops early can’t be making a note that keeps going.
June never heard Agnes, but she heard the note by the water. Where does that put the note?

lines.text: Count the nights, Steven. And when you record them, leave room for the loud parts.

bait.finding: steve|The low note comes from the water, under the floating dock. Agnes only hums along. June heard it without her. And it is the note under Mom’s voicemail.

recap: steve|Admiral turned away from Nora’s whistle. Lyle Boone apologized to me. And the bay is humming the note that has been under Mom’s voice for eighteen months.
steve|One odd thing is an accident. Three is a list.
steve|Dinner at La Marea was at six. Carmen has kept my plate warm every Sunday since the boat. She throws it out every Monday.

lines: steve|How old is he now?
iris|Nine. He weighs more than your car.
steve|You bottle-fed him in our bathtub. For three weeks.
iris|I remember. It was a good bathtub.
iris|The line is long today. The crab boats came in early.
steve|You used to talk your way to the front of that line.
iris|Waiting is fine. Everyone gets a turn.
steve|You still whistle for him every Sunday?
iris|Every Sunday. Two notes. He always comes.
steve|You used to say he’d come to that whistle through a hurricane.
iris|Then you should visit him more often, sleepyhead.
steve|How’s business, Mrs. Penhallow?
agnes|Splendid. Nobody has bought a thing since Tuesday.
steve|That’s splendid?
agnes|It means the fish are safe, Steven. Somebody has to be on their side.
steve|You still remember me from third grade?
agnes|You took my classroom clock apart to find the tick.
steve|I put it back together.
agnes|With two pieces left over. It ran fast ever after.
steve|Halibut again, June?
calder|Every Sunday for twenty years. My mother bought it in this same line.
calder|Some things in this town don’t change. I like that about it.
steve|Is that Lyle by the shed? In a clean shirt?
calder|He asked for every Sunday off this summer. For his boys’ games.
calder|Since early summer he’s been my best deputy. Never late once. I keep waiting for the catch.
steve|Who’s pitching first today?
lyle_copy|My oldest, then his brother. I’ll be in the stands for every inning.
steve|You sound sure.
lyle_copy|I made them a promise. I keep my promises now.
steve|Mail on a Sunday, Dale?
pell|Every route runs on schedule, Mr. Mercer.
steve|There’s no Sunday route.
pell|There is today.

c1_dinner.when: Sunday the 21st, six in the evening
c1_dinner.coach: Some leads ask for settings. Pick one choice on each row, then press Apply settings. Each row shows if it is right. Click people at the table to chat.
c1_dinner.objective: Have dinner with Nora’s family, and listen to the people who know her best.
notes: Art (recommended): an insert of Carmen’s birthday photo strip pinned by the register, three snapshots of Nora stamped 20:04, 20:15 (holding the kitchen check) and 20:29, in the style of inserts/c1_pier.webp.
The photo times and drivers are needed again in c1_escape.order.
context: steve|La Marea. The Reyes family restaurant, and for four years my Sunday table.
steve|Luis still keeps Dad’s old chair at the bar. Nobody sits in it.

intro.text: Your plate is warm, Steve. Sit. I’m her mother, so you can apologize to me while you eat.

intro: carmen|Nora, the mole. More chilies this time, or less?

intro.text: Whatever you think is best, Mamá.

intro: tomas|She used to call it a crime against chilies.
tomas|She texts like a ransom note, too. No capitals. No apostrophes.

birthday.title: Carmen’s photo strip
birthday.goal: Write down where Nora was on Carmen’s birthday, and who saw her.
birthday.background: Carmen photographs everything, mostly food, and her camera stamps the time on every picture. Nora is in three of last month’s birthday photos: 20:04, 20:15 with the kitchen check in her hand, and 20:29.
lead: carmen|Look at this. My birthday, last month.
carmen|Your girl agreed with me all night. Eleven times. I counted.

lead.text: I drove her here at noon. Rafa drove her home. Midnight, give or take ten minutes.

birthday.prompt: Steve puts a date on everything. What can he write down for certain?
options: Nora was at La Marea at 20:04, 20:15 and 20:29; Mateo drove her in at noon, and Rafa drove her home at midnight
Nora never left the restaurant all day

wrong.1: The photos cover twenty-five minutes. Mateo and Rafa cover the ends. Nobody watched her every minute.
wrong.2: She’s smiling in every picture. Smiles don’t come with timestamps.

hints: Separate what the photos show from what anyone assumes.
Each photo fixes one moment. The two rides fix the start and the end.
Keep only what has a time stamp or a witness behind it.
lines: c1_dinner.out.01
birthday.finding: steve|Carmen’s birthday: Nora at La Marea at 20:04, 20:15 and 20:29. Mateo drove her in at noon. Rafa drove her home at midnight.

family.title: When did she change?
family.background: Steve worked nights all spring and summer. He can’t say when Nora changed, because he had stopped looking. Her brothers can. Each of them remembers a last argument or a first surprise.
lead: steve|When did she stop arguing? With any of you?
mateo|With me? She fought me about her driving every week. The last real fight was Memorial Day weekend.
rafa|She sent my mole back every Sunday for ten years. Too sweet. The first Sunday in June, she ate the whole plate.
tomas|She called my show every episode to fix my tide tables. The last call was May seventeenth.
mateo|Funny. Lyle Boone hasn’t missed one of the Little League games I coach since June either.
family.prompt: Nora changed after her last argument and before the first time she simply agreed. Bracket it.
family.instruction: Pick the last argument anyone remembers. Then pick the first time she just agreed.

rows.label: Last argument anyone remembers
options: Mateo’s driving fight, Memorial Day weekend

hints: Look for the latest argument and the earliest agreement.
Tomás’s call came before Mateo’s fight. Carmen’s birthday came long after Rafa’s mole.
Put the dates in order: May 17, Memorial Day weekend, the first Sunday in June, Carmen’s birthday in September. The change sits in one gap.

lines.text: Eat before it gets cold, Steve. Then tell us what is troubling you.

lines: steve|I’m not sure yet, Luis. I’m working on it.
family.finding: steve|Nora stopped arguing with her family between the end of May and the first Sunday in June. Lyle changed in June too. I was on nights. I never noticed.

podcast.title: Tomás’s field reels
podcast.goal: Find out whether the hum in the bay keeps a schedule.
podcast.background: Nora’s brother Tomás, twenty-nine, has said for three years that something is hiding in the bay. Nobody listens, Steve included. His podcast is cut up for drama, but his field reels are dated in pencil, and he only goes out on the nights the hum is loudest.
lead: tomas|Steve. You’re the sound guy. Settle something. There’s a hum in the bay. Three years of tape, and nobody listens.
steve|I heard it today. On the pier.
tomas|...You heard it?
podcast.prompt: Tomás will lend Steve his field reels if Steve can file them back by date. If the hum keeps a schedule, the dates will show it.

board.instruction: Match each reel to its date. Then count the nights between dates to find the next loud night.
evidence: September 24: the bell buoy was in the water, ringing at low tide.
October 3: the buoy was ashore for repair, with a cracked clapper. It could not ring.
October 12: the repair crew tapped the buoy twice, then put it back in the water.
Each reel starts with whatever was making noise when Tomás pressed record.
Tomás only goes out on the nights the hum is loudest. September has thirty days.

stages.prompt: Match each date to the first sound on its reel.
Count the nights between the dates. When is the next loud night?

board.wrong_text: Tomás squints at the crate. Something here doesn’t match his log.

hints: Where was the buoy on October 3? Could it ring that night?
Count the nights from one date to the next. September has thirty days.
September 24 to October 3 is the same count as October 3 to October 12. Add that count once more.
lines: c1_dinner.podcast.01
c1_dinner.podcast.02
podcast.finding: steve|Tomás’s loud nights come every nine nights: September 24, October 3, October 12. The next one is tonight.

recap: steve|Nora changed between the end of May and the first Sunday in June. Lyle changed in June. Carmen noticed. Admiral noticed. I didn’t.
steve|And Tomás has three years of tape that says the bay hums every nine nights. Tonight is the ninth.
outro: iris|I’m tired. Let’s go home, sleepyhead.
carmen|Next Sunday, Steve. The plate will be warm.

lines: steve|The mole is perfect, Carmen.
carmen|It is too sweet. Rafa is in love, so everything he cooks is sweet now.
steve|Rafa’s in love?
carmen|With the girl from the bakery counter. He thinks I don’t know. Mothers know.
steve|You still keep Dad’s chair, Luis.
luis|Frank sat there every Friday for twenty years. Nobody else fits it.
luis|When he comes home, it will be waiting for him.
steve|Thanks, Luis.
steve|How’s the team, Mateo?
mateo|Four wins, nine losses. But we lead the league in effort.
mateo|And my outfield can finally catch. Mostly with their faces, but it counts.
steve|Busy night, Rafa?
rafa|Forty tables, one birthday, and Mamá tasting everything twice.
rafa|Come to Sunday dinner for real, Steve. She sets your plate either way.
steve|How’s the podcast, Tomás?
tomas|Eleven listeners. Twelve, if Mamá ever figures out the app.
tomas|Laugh now. One day the bay is going to make me famous.
tomas|Come on my show sometime, Steve. A real sound engineer would double my ratings.
steve|From twelve listeners to twenty-four?
tomas|Nora used to call in every week just to correct my tide tables. I miss that, honestly.
steve|You’re quiet tonight, Nor.
iris|I’m happy. Everyone is here.
steve|You used to argue with your mother about the chilies all night.
iris|Mamá knows best.

c1_escape.coach: Steve’s notebook keeps every clue you have found. Press J to look things up when a case board needs an earlier fact.
notes: Objective changes to the next step once c1_escape.order is solved.
Art (recommended): an insert of the rain-soaked work order, Bellwether Aquarium letterhead, NORTH WING, signed N. Reyes, wall-clock time 20:30, dated on Carmen’s birthday.
context: steve|Home. Nora took a phone call in the bedroom and closed the door. She never closes the door.
steve|Her raincoat was dripping on the floor. I carried it out to hang on the balcony hooks.

order.title: The paper in the raincoat
order.goal: Work out whether Nora could have signed this work order.
order.background: Something stiff fell out of the raincoat lining when Steve hung it on the balcony hook: an aquarium work order for the north wing, sealed for two years. Only the head aquarist signs for it, and that is Nora. It is signed in her name on Carmen’s birthday, at 20:30 by the aquarium wall clock.
lead: steve|Something in the lining. Soaked. Aquarium letterhead... north wing?
steve|Signed at 20:30. Nora always said that north-wing clock runs fifteen minutes fast.
steve|And the aquarium is across the bay. Eighteen minutes each way, even with every light green.
order.prompt: Steve’s notes from dinner put Nora at La Marea that evening. Could she have slipped away to sign this?

board.instruction: First fix the time on the work order. Then check whether Nora had time for the trip.
evidence: The work order says 20:30 by the aquarium clock.
The aquarium clock runs fifteen minutes fast.
Carmen’s photos show Nora at La Marea at 20:04, 20:15 and 20:29. At 20:15 she is holding the kitchen check.
Crossing the bay takes eighteen minutes each way.

stages.prompt: When was the order really signed, and where was Nora then?
slots: Where Nora was at that time
pieces: At La Marea, in Carmen’s photo

stages.prompt: Could she get there and back between two photos?
pieces: Nora could not have signed it

board.wrong_text: Something here doesn’t fit the clock or the photos yet.

hints: The aquarium clock runs fast. Take the extra minutes off.
The real signing time matches one of Carmen’s photos.
Add up the trip there and back. Is any gap between photos that long?

lines.text: Noon to midnight at La Marea. Mateo and Rafa both saw her. She couldn’t have been in the north wing.

lines: steve|What notebook?

lines.text: Nora? The balcony door’s locked. From inside.

order.finding: steve|Someone signed Nora’s name in the north wing while she was at her mother’s birthday, across the bay. And now Nora has locked me out on the balcony.
order.note: Someone used Nora’s name in the north wing while she was at dinner. Nora locked Steve out on the balcony.

power.title: Mr. Bell’s gate
lead: steve|Mr. Bell’s gate. It’s the only way down from here.
power.goal: Open Mr. Bell’s balcony gate without turning off his stair light.
power.background: The only way off the balcony is along the shared rail to Mr. Bell’s gate. Mr. Bell is eighty-four and halfway down the dark communal stairs with his groceries. Steve rewired this gate last winter and was paid in fruitcake.
power.prompt: Open Mr. Bell’s gate without ever darkening the stair light. The service selector has three positions.
power.instruction: NORMAL: stair light on, gate motor on. SERVICE: light on, motor off. OFF: everything off. The gate pad only holds a press while the motor is off and your thumb stays down. The motor checks the pad when it switches on.

rows.label: While the pad is still pressed

hints: Track two things separately: the stair bulb and the gate motor.
The pad only remembers a press while the motor is off, and the motor checks the pad as it switches on. Which position keeps the bulb lit with the motor off?
The pad has to be pressed while the motor is off and the bulb is on, and still pressed at the moment the motor switches on.
lines: c1_escape.power.01
power.finding: steve|Mr. Bell’s gate opened, and his stair light never flickered. He never knew I was there.

cross.title: Nora’s irises
cross.background: The shared rail runs past Nora’s pots of irises to Mr. Bell’s open gate and the lit stair. The crash brings Nora to the balcony door.
options: Climb along the rail toward the stair
hints: There is nothing to solve here.
There is nothing to solve here.
Climb along the rail toward the stair.
lines: c1_escape.cross.01
iris|Steve.
steve|Don’t. Please. I don’t know who you are tonight.
cross.finding: steve|She was close enough to stop me. She didn’t move.
cross.note: Nora watched Steve go and did nothing to stop him.

recap: steve|My list: one good morning, played twice. A whistle Admiral won’t answer. A signature Nora couldn’t have made. A phone call about a notebook. A locked door.
steve|And Tomás’s tapes say the bay sings tonight.
steve|So I went down to the beach. In Bellwether, that’s where you go when you can’t sleep.

outro.new: steve|Midnight. That’s Lyle, in his church shoes. Gus from the bakery. They’re walking into the water.
